848.title: flowers on the man who lost
848.hook: the war is won, the teacher raises his plough at the winner, and flowers fall on the man who lost
848.carry: svadharma: even Duryodhana's courage is counted
848.howItsDone: The mace fight and its aftermath are told in recitations and retellings of the Mahabharata, and some retellings give Duryodhana a measure of honor in defeat.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna struck his own thigh, and Bhima's forbidden blow broke Duryodhana's. Your line was dharmakshetra: life is the field of dharma.

Duryodhana lies on the ground and can't get up. The fight is over. The Pandavas have won the war. And for a moment, nobody behaves the way winners are supposed to. Bhima walks over to the fallen king and puts his foot on his head. Yudhishthira, his own brother, tells him to stop. And Balarama, the teacher who trained both fighters, is so angry at the blow he just saw that he lifts his plough, his own weapon, and runs at Bhima. The victory itself is put on trial.
screen: `THE KING CAN'T RISE.` → `A FOOT ON HIS HEAD.` → `THE TEACHER CHARGES.`

segments.voice: In Ganguli's telling, Yudhishthira tells Bhima the foot does him no honor. Krishna catches hold of Balarama and reminds him of Bhima's vow from the dice hall, but Balarama leaves for Dvaraka in anger. Then the fallen king turns on Krishna and lists the deaths he calls unfair: Bhishma, Drona, Karna. Krishna answers with a list of his own: the poison, the house of lac, the dice, Draupadi dragged into the hall. Your own wrongs brought you here. Duryodhana answers that he lived as a king should: he ruled, he gave, he fought and never ran. And flowers rain down on him from the sky. Music sounds. The Pandavas stand there downcast. Here's the teaching under the flowers. Hindus speak of svadharma, your own dharma, the duty that belongs to your place in life. For a warrior, the Gita says, death in battle opens heaven. Duryodhana did terrible wrong, and his wrongs brought him down. But he also kept a warrior's dharma to the very end, and the epic counts that too. At the close of the whole Mahabharata, Yudhishthira reaches heaven and is furious to find Duryodhana already there, and he's told this is why. The epic won't let anyone be only a villain. Most of us keep a short list of people we've cast as the bad guy. The Hindu view doesn't erase what they did; it asks you to see the dharma they kept as well.

Breathing out, let both be true at once, the way the epic lets flowers fall on Duryodhana. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.

849.title: a commander made in grief
849.hook: three men are all that's left of an army, and a dying king makes one of them its commander
849.carry: krodha, anger, is an enemy within
849.howItsDone: Sauptika, from a Sanskrit word for sleep, is the name of the tenth of the Mahabharata's eighteen books, and reciters of the whole epic carry the story straight on from the fallen king into the night raid.

segments.voice: Yesterday: flowers fell on Duryodhana for the warrior's dharma he kept. Your line was svadharma, even Duryodhana's courage is counted.

Evening on the battlefield. Three warriors come looking for their king: Ashvatthama, the son of Drona; Kripa, the old teacher of the princes; and Kritavarma, a fighter from Krishna's own clan who fought on the other side. They're the last of the Kaurava army still standing. They find Duryodhana where Bhima left him, his thighs broken, covered in dust, unable to rise. The man who once commanded a vast host now has three men and a darkening sky. This is Sauptika, the book of the night.
screen: `THREE WARRIORS LEFT.` → `THEY FIND THEIR KING.` → `THE BOOK OF THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: In Ganguli's telling, the three weep at the sight of him. Duryodhana, in pain, still speaks like a king: don't grieve; I fought and didn't turn my back. But Ashvatthama can't let it rest. He remembers how his own father died: told a lie about his son's death, laying down his weapons, and then killed. Now he sees his king broken by a blow below the waist. And he makes a vow, in effect: before this night is over, I'll send the Panchalas to the land of the dead. Then Duryodhana, who can't stand and has no army, asks Kripa for a pot of water, and with it has Kripa install Ashvatthama as commander. Commander of three men. Ashvatthama embraces the king, and the three go off into the night. Hindu teachers have a name for what was just crowned. They speak of six inner enemies, the shadripu: desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy. The second is krodha, anger. It isn't an enemy out there. It lives inside, and it can borrow grief's face, so it feels like loyalty, like love for a father or a king. Ashvatthama's grief is real. But tonight it's anger that takes command, with a vow and a pot of water. It's the same for us when someone hurts a person we love: the hottest promises come in the first hour. The teaching doesn't say don't grieve. It says notice who's giving the orders.
screen: `THEY WEEP OVER THE KING` · `ASHVATTHAMA'S VOW` · `A COMMANDER OF THREE` · then, large: `KRODHA, THE ENEMY WITHIN`

segments.voice: Sit and feel where heat collects when you're angry: the chest, the jaw, the hands. Many Hindus close their prayers with om shanti shanti shanti, peace said three times. Breathing in, notice the heat without feeding it. Breathing out, say shanti silently: once for your body, once for your words, once for whoever you're angry with. If you don't pray, let the word simply mean peace.

Your line: krodha, anger, is an enemy within. Tomorrow, under a banyan tree, one man can't sleep. That's day eight hundred forty-nine.

850.title: the owl and the crows
850.hook: two men sleep under a banyan tree, and the third lies awake watching an owl hunt
850.carry: from anger comes confusion, the Gita warns
850.howItsDone: The owl among the crows appears in retellings and illustrated editions of the Mahabharata when they tell the night raid.

segments.voice: Yesterday: in his grief, Ashvatthama vowed revenge and was made commander of three. Your line was krodha, anger, is an enemy within.

A huge banyan tree in a forest at night, its branches full of sleeping crows. Under it, three tired warriors have stopped to rest. They've ridden away from the field, afraid the Pandavas might find them. Kripa lies down and sleeps. Kritavarma sleeps too; they've been fighting for days. But Ashvatthama can't sleep. He lies on the ground with his eyes open, burning, the text says, with anger and grief. And up in the branches, something moves.
screen: `A BANYAN FULL OF CROWS.` → `TWO MEN SLEEP.` → `ONE LIES AWAKE.`

segments.voice: In Ganguli's telling, an owl comes down through the dark, large and fierce, with sharp talons, and lands among the sleeping crows. One by one, it kills them. The crows never wake in time to fly. Ashvatthama watches the whole thing, and says to himself, in effect: this owl has taught me something. The Pandavas can't be beaten in open battle. But tonight they'll be asleep. Notice: no god speaks, no adviser plots. The owl only hunted. It was Ashvatthama who made it a plan. Hindus know a famous teaching about exactly this. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna traces a ladder downward. Brooding on a thing brings attachment; attachment brings desire; desire, blocked, turns to anger. From anger comes confusion. From confusion, memory slips. And when memory slips, buddhi, the power to judge, is lost, and with it the person. Many readers watch Ashvatthama go down that ladder under the banyan: grief, then anger, then a mind that can no longer tell a sign from a wish. For us, it's the hour after midnight, when a hurt feels like proof and everything seems to point to the thing you already wanted to do. The Gita's answer isn't to stop feeling. It's to notice which rung you're on, and not to decide anything there.

851.title: Kripa's counsel in the dark
851.hook: an old teacher is shaken awake in the dark and told the plan, and he tries to talk his nephew out of it
851.carry: fate and effort work together; ask the elders
851.howItsDone: Kripa's counsel under the banyan, with its talk of fate and human effort working together, is a passage some readers return to when they think about fate and action in the Mahabharata.

segments.voice: Yesterday: an owl killed the sleeping crows, and anger read it as a plan. Your line was from anger comes confusion, the Gita warns.

Kripa opens his eyes. It's still dark. His nephew is standing over him, and so is Kritavarma, who's been woken too. Ashvatthama tells them what he saw in the tree and what he means to do: go to the Pandava camp tonight, while everyone sleeps, and kill the men who killed his father. Kripa is old. He taught the princes on both sides when they were boys, and he has fought this whole war beside Duryodhana. Now, half awake under a banyan, he has a few minutes to change his nephew's mind.
screen: `KRIPA IS WOKEN.` → `THE PLAN IS SPOKEN.` → `A FEW MINUTES TO ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Kripa doesn't shout. In Ganguli's telling he starts with a teaching Hindu thinkers return to again and again: daiva and purushakara, what fate gives and what a person does. Success needs both together. Effort alone isn't enough, and neither is fate. Then he gets practical. Don't decide this alone, he says, in effect. Let's go to Dhritarashtra, to Gandhari, to the wise Vidura, and ask them what should be done. And he names the thing directly: killing men who are asleep is not honored in this world. Ashvatthama has an answer for everything. The Panchalas broke the rules first, he says. Dhrishtadyumna killed my father while he sat with his weapons laid down. He cannot sleep while they live, and he doesn't care if he's reborn as a worm or an insect for it. Then he yokes his horses, and Kripa and Kritavarma, who argued against him, follow. So here's the teaching under the banyan. Hindus don't believe in sitting back and calling it fate; effort matters. But effort has to be joined to the right time and to wise counsel. That's why Hindu families take big decisions to their elders, and ask a blessing before they begin. Kripa offered exactly that, and it was refused. When you're sure you have to act right now, Kripa's counsel is the old one: do the work, but not alone, and not before you've asked the people who love you.
screen: `DAIVA AND PURUSHAKARA` · `ASK THE ELDERS FIRST` · `"THEY BROKE THE RULES FIRST"` · then, large: `THEY FOLLOW HIM ANYWAY`

852.title: the being at the gate
852.hook: a gigantic being blocks the gate of the sleeping camp, and every weapon Ashvatthama throws disappears into it
852.carry: Shiva ends what has had its time
852.tomorrow: the night the Pandavas were away
852.howItsDone: Hindus who worship Shiva as Mahadeva call on him by many names, and the hymn Ashvatthama offers at the gate is one of the places in the Mahabharata where those names are gathered.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kripa named fate and effort, begged his nephew to ask the elders, lost, and followed anyway. Your line was fate and effort work together; ask the elders.

The Pandava camp is dark and quiet. Ashvatthama reaches the gate with Kripa and Kritavarma behind him. And the gate isn't empty. Something is standing there, so large it seems to fill the night. In Ganguli's English it's a being of enormous size, terrible to look at, blazing, wrapped in a tiger skin, with snakes for ornaments and many eyes. It doesn't speak. It just stands between Ashvatthama and the sleeping camp.
screen: `THE CAMP IS ASLEEP.` → `A BEING AT THE GATE.` → `IT DOESN'T SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Ashvatthama does what a warrior does. He attacks. He hurls weapon after weapon at the being, and it swallows them all and stands untouched. Empty-handed, he thinks of the advice he ignored, in effect: whoever turns from the counsel of friends who wish him well comes to grief. Then he turns to Mahadeva, the great god, Shiva, and praises him with many names. A golden altar appears with a fire blazing on it, and Shiva's fierce companions crowd around. Ashvatthama offers the only thing he has left, himself, and steps into the fire. Shiva appears and speaks plainly: he has protected the Panchalas until now, out of regard for Krishna, but their time is over. He gives Ashvatthama a sword and enters into him. Here's why this matters for Hindus. Shiva is the god who brings things to an end. Many Hindus speak of God's three great works: Brahma creates, Vishnu sustains, Shiva dissolves. That last work isn't evil. It clears the ground for what comes next, which is why Shiva is also called Mahakala, great Time, and why he is honored at the cremation ground, where a life is given back. In this book, Shiva says a time has ended. But the epic doesn't let Ashvatthama hide behind that: in two days, Krishna will hold him answerable. So a Hindu can say two things at once. Endings belong to God. What we do in them still belongs to us.
screen: `THE WEAPONS VANISH` · `HE OFFERS HIMSELF` · `"THEIR TIME IS OVER"` · then, large: `SHIVA, LORD OF ENDINGS`

segments.voice: Om namah shivaya is one of the most loved prayers in Hinduism: a bow to Shiva. Sit tall and bring to mind something in your life that is ending, or has ended. Breathing slowly, say the prayer silently, once on each out-breath, and let the ending be held by something larger than you. If you don't pray, breathe out slowly and simply let the ending be named.

Dhrishtadyumna is asleep in his tent, on a fine bed, the commander of the Pandava army resting after the war he helped win. He is the man who killed Drona. He wakes because someone is standing on him. It's Ashvatthama, Drona's son. This is the night the whole book is named for, and the epic tells it without looking away. Here it's told more gently, holding on to the few moments the text slows down for: a request, a refusal, and a message brought to a dying king.
screen: `A COMMANDER ASLEEP.` → `DRONA'S SON STANDS OVER HIM.` → `THE NIGHT ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Dhrishtadyumna, pinned down, asks for one thing. In Ganguli's telling he begs to be killed with a weapon, so that he dies as a warrior. Ashvatthama refuses: a man who killed his teacher, he says in effect, doesn't deserve a warrior's death. Then he moves through the camp. Others wake and fall: Shikhandi, Uttamaujas, Yudhamanyu, and the five young sons of Draupadi, who came to the war with their fathers. Kripa and Kritavarma stand at the gate, and fire is set to the camp. Back on the field, Duryodhana hears what they've done, and dies. But the Pandava brothers aren't in the camp. Neither are Krishna or Satyaki. Earlier that evening, Krishna had taken them to spend the night elsewhere. The men Ashvatthama most wanted were never there. Now the teaching. Hindus speak of karma: every action bears fruit, as surely as a seed. Watch the seeds in this war. Drona was brought down with a lie. His son answers with killing in the dark. And the fruit falls on Draupadi's sons, who did none of it. Ashvatthama thought he was settling an account; he was planting the next one, and tomorrow it comes due for him. When someone hurts us, it's tempting to say karma will get them, and then to help it along. The epic's answer is hard and clear: karma isn't a weapon you aim. The moment you aim, the deed is yours, and so is its fruit.

Morning. Dhrishtadyumna's charioteer, one of the few who got away, brings the news to Yudhishthira, and the king falls to the ground. Then Draupadi comes. Her brother is dead. Her five sons are dead. She sits down in front of her husbands and says she'll take no food until Ashvatthama pays for this. And she names what she wants. Ashvatthama was born with a jewel on his head. She wants to see it brought back, and worn by Yudhishthira.
screen: `THE NEWS AT DAWN.` → `DRAUPADI SITS DOWN.` → `SHE ASKS FOR THE JEWEL.`

segments.voice: Bhima rides out at once. Krishna warns that Drona once taught his son a terrible weapon, the Brahmashira, and Ashvatthama is reckless enough to use it. So Krishna, Arjuna and Yudhishthira follow. They find Ashvatthama on the bank of the Ganga, among sages, with Vyasa. He charges a blade of grass with that weapon and lets it go. Arjuna answers with the same. Two fires rise, and the sages Narada and Vyasa step between them to save the world. Arjuna, who has kept his vows, calls his weapon back. Ashvatthama can't. He turns it toward the unborn heirs of the Pandavas, and Krishna answers that Uttara's child will live, because Krishna will revive him. Then Krishna curses Ashvatthama to wander the earth alone for a very long time, and Ashvatthama gives up the jewel he was born with. Now watch Draupadi. Her brother and her sons are dead. In Ganguli's telling she says, in effect, that she only wanted the wrong answered, and that a teacher's son deserves the reverence due the teacher. She takes the jewel, not his life, and gives it to Yudhishthira to wear. The Bhagavata Purana tells it more tenderly still: there Draupadi asks that he be spared, so his mother won't weep as she is weeping. Hindus call this kshama, forgiveness, and count it among the great virtues. It doesn't pretend the wrong didn't happen. It asks what needs to be answered, and lets the rest go.
